claim: Physicists have been sharing preprints using the service now called arXiv.org since 1991.

source: Among the 30 journals publishing the most bioRxiv preprints, the journal with the most rapid transition from bioRxiv to publication is G3, whose median, 119 days, is significantly different from all journals except Genetics, mBio, and The Biophysical Journal (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides journal-specific publication interval data.

claim: G3's median publication interval is significantly different from all journals except Genetics, mBio, and The Biophysical Journal.
source: Among the 30 journals publishing the most bioRxiv preprints, the journal with the most rapid transition from bioRxiv to publication is G3, whose median, 119 days, is significantly different from all journals except Genetics, mBio, and The Biophysical Journal (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparisons of G3's publication interval to other journals.

claim: 122 preprints were published within a week of being posted to bioRxiv.
source: For example, 122 preprints were published within a week of being posted to bioRxiv, and the longest period between preprint and publication is 3 years, 7 months and 2 days, for a preprint that was posted in March 2015 and not published until October 2018 (Figure 6a).
evidence: The manuscript provides data on the range of publication intervals.

claim: The longest period between preprint and publication is 3 years, 7 months and 2 days, for a preprint posted in March 2015 and published in October 2018.

claim: An average paper can receive hundreds of downloads in its first few months online.
source: For authors, particularly those looking for feedback from the community, our results show bioRxiv preprints are being downloaded more than one million times per month, and that an average paper can receive hundreds of downloads in its first few months online (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes download patterns for typical preprints.

claim: Serghiou and Ioannidis (2018) found an almost identical median for downloads in a preprint's first month.
source: Serghiou and Ioannidis (2018) evaluated download metrics for bioRxiv preprints through 2016 and found an almost identical median for downloads in a preprint's first month; we have expanded this to include more detailed longitudinal traffic metrics for the entire bioRxiv collection (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript compares their findings to a previous study.

claim: The vast majority of final published papers are largely indistinguishable from their pre-print versions.
source: In short, the majority of bioRxiv preprints do appear in journals eventually, and potentially with very few differences: an analysis of published preprints that had first been posted to arXiv.org found that 'the vast majority of final published papers are largely indistinguishable from their pre-print versions' (Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Klein et al., 2016 for this finding about preprint-publication similarity.

claim: Among preprints that are eventually published, 75% have appeared in a journal by the time they had spent 247 days on bioRxiv.
source: Among preprints that are eventually published, we found that 75% have appeared in a journal by the time they had spent 247 days (about eight months) on bioRxiv.
evidence: The manuscript provides quartile data on publication timing.

claim: Preprints on arXiv were most frequently published within a year of being posted there.
source: This interval is similar to results from Larivière et al. showing preprints on arXiv were most frequently published within a year of being posted there (Larivière et al., 2014), and to a later study examining bioRxiv preprints that found 'the probability of publication in the peer-reviewed literature was 48% within 12 months' (Serghiou and Ioannidis, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Larivière et al., 2014 for comparison with arXiv publication intervals.

claim: A study found the probability of publication in the peer-reviewed literature was 48% within 12 months for bioRxiv preprints.
source: This interval is similar to results from Larivière et al. showing preprints on arXiv were most frequently published within a year of being posted there (Larivière et al., 2014), and to a later study examining bioRxiv preprints that found 'the probability of publication in the peer-reviewed literature was 48% within 12 months' (Serghiou and Ioannidis, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Serghiou and Ioannidis, 2018 for this publication probability finding.

claim: A study published in spring 2017 found that 33.6% of preprints from 2015 and earlier had been published.

evidence: The manuscript cites Schloss, 2017 for comparison with their updated findings.

evidence: The manuscript provides updated publication rate data for older preprints.

claim: A paper's presence on bioRxiv has a relationship to its eventual citation count once published in a journal, as has been found with arXiv.
source: Does a paper's presence on bioRxiv have any relationship to its eventual citation count once it is published in a journal, as has been found with arXiv (e.g. Feldman et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Schwarz and Kennicutt, 2004)?
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies showing this relationship for arXiv preprints.

claim: There is a significant association between Twitter mentions of published papers and their citation counts.

claim: Only 17.8% of bioRxiv papers had an 'open license'.

evidence: The manuscript cites Himmelstein, 2016b for this finding about open licensing.

claim: Beginning in September 2018, bioRxiv held more biology preprints than all other major preprint servers combined.
source: Using these resources, researchers can now perform detailed and robust bibliometric analysis of the website with the largest collection of preprints in biology, the one that, beginning in September 2018, held more biology preprints than all other major preprint servers combined (Anaya, 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites Anaya, 2018 for this comparison of preprint server sizes.

claim: BioRxiv has compensated for a low rate of comments posted on the site itself by highlighting external sources such as tweets and blogs.
source: While bioRxiv has compensated for a low rate of comments posted on the site itself (Inglis and Sever, 2016) by highlighting external sources such as tweets and blogs, Rxivist provides additional context for how a preprint compares to others on similar topics.
evidence: The manuscript cites Inglis and Sever, 2016 for information about bioRxiv's comment rate.

claim: A Python-based web crawler was developed to visit every content page on the bioRxiv website and download basic data about each preprint.
